claims.text: An optimized ultrathin CeO2 overcoat will improve the low-temperature catalytic activity of the multi-element automotive high-entropy catalyst.
An optimized ultrathin CeO2 overcoat will improve catalyst durability under transient exhaust conditions.
Oxygen buffering and electronic modification by the CeO2 overcoat will stabilize active sites against poisoning and thermal aging.
The starting material is a nearly equiatomic, multi-element high-entropy alloy catalyst containing only trace amounts of platinum-group metals.
Vapor deposition of approximately 1–2 at% Ce followed by calcination at about 250 °C in air will form an ultrathin, coherent CeO2 overcoat.
The CeO2 overcoat will be intimately bonded to the native high-entropy catalyst surface.
The ultrathin CeO2 layer will provide oxygen storage and buffering.
CeO2 will buffer reactive oxygen species and moderate the local oxygen chemical potential.
Oxygen buffering by the CeO2 layer will protect active metal sites from poisoning by H2O and NO.
The CeO2 layer will minimize thermal degradation of the catalyst.
Electronic interaction between CeO2 and the underlying alloy will adjust the adsorption energies of reaction intermediates.
The adjusted adsorption energies will increase catalytic turnover while preventing deactivation.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the CeO2-coated catalyst will have superior low-temperature activity, durability, poisoning resistance, and thermal-aging resistance.
The proposed intervention will maintain low platinum-group-metal usage.
The untreated multi-element catalyst typically undergoes rapid activity loss under transient low-temperature exhaust operation, repeated H2O/NO exposure, and thermal aging.
A CeO2 layer that is too thick will block active sites and eliminate the performance benefit.
A CeO2 layer that is too thin will provide insufficient oxygen buffering and eliminate the performance benefit.
The performance benefit is expected during cyclic exhaust simulation at approximately 200–250 °C with controlled H2O and NO exposure.
The optimal overcoat thickness, long-term cycling stability, scale-up uniformity, and particle-to-particle reproducibility remain uncertain.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement over an untreated control, or a decline caused by reduced active-site accessibility, will falsify the hypothesis.
